passages.happening:
Tax collectors and sinners are all gathering around to listen to Jesus. The Pharisees and scribes grumble: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (verse 2).

So Jesus tells them a parable. Which of you, if you had a hundred sheep and lost one, would not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost one “until he finds it?” (verse 4). When he finds it, he puts it on his shoulders with joy, comes home, and calls his friends and neighbours: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!” (verse 6).

“In the same way, I tell you that there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is one answer to one complaint, told as three stories: a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son. Luke calls it ‘this parable’, as if the three were one.

The complaint is about meals. Tax collectors worked for the rulers, Herod's family or Rome, and were widely hated as cheats (see the note on 3:12-14). ‘Sinners’ meant people whose lives openly broke God's law. To eat with someone in that world was to accept them, in front of everyone. The Pharisees, who took great care over what and with whom they ate, were shocked that a teacher would share a table with such people. They had made the same complaint before (5:30). Jesus does not deny it. He tells them why.

He begins, ‘What man among you’. He asks the critics to imagine themselves as the shepherd. A hundred sheep was a fair-sized flock for an ordinary family. Any shepherd would go after a lost one. A sheep alone in the hills is helpless.

Notice the joy. The shepherd does not scold the sheep or drive it home with a stick. He carries it on his shoulders, and then he throws a party. Jesus says heaven is like that. The Pharisees were grumbling over the very thing heaven celebrates.

Matthew tells the lost sheep too, in a different setting (Matthew 18:12-14). There Jesus tells it to his disciples, and the sheep ‘goes astray’; the story is a charge to the church not to let a wandering believer go. Here he tells it to his critics, and the sheep is ‘lost’. In Luke the shepherd searches ‘until he finds it’. In Matthew it is ‘if he finds it’.
passages.ot:
The shepherd was an old picture of God. “He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart” (Isaiah 40:11).

Through Ezekiel God condemned Israel's leaders for failing the flock, and promised to search for them himself: “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16). When Jesus goes looking for the lost, he is doing what God said he would do.
passages.hard:
Who are the ‘ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent’? Jesus may be speaking with a touch of irony, using the critics' own picture of themselves. Or he may mean that the faithful are truly loved, but that the lost one is where heaven's eyes are turned for now. Readers take it both ways. Either way, the verse does not say that anyone is so good that they are beyond needing God. Its point is the joy over the one who comes home.

Does the shepherd not care about the ninety-nine? He leaves them in the open country, which seems a risk. But the story is not about farming. It is about what kind of love God has: a love that counts one as worth the search.
passages.asks: Ask whom you are quietly glad to keep away from the table. Then ask whether you share heaven's joy when they come near, or the Pharisees' grumbling. And if you are the one who has wandered, notice that the shepherd does not wait for the sheep to find its own way back. He comes looking.

passages.t: The lost coin, and the woman who searched
passages.happening:
Or what woman, if she has ten silver coins and loses one, does not “light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it?” (verse 8). When she finds it, she calls her friends and neighbours together: ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin’ (verse 9).

“In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story.

The coins were silver drachmas, Greek coins worth about the same as a Roman denarius, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. Ten of them was not a fortune, but for a poor household it was a great deal. Losing one meant real loss.

She lights a lamp to see into the corners, sweeps the floor to hear the coin or catch its glint, and searches carefully. Then she calls her women friends and neighbours together to share her joy. The Greek words for ‘friends’ and ‘neighbours’ here are feminine.

Jesus has just pictured God as a shepherd. Now he pictures God as a woman sweeping her house. Luke often sets a story about a woman beside a story about a man, as with the mustard seed and the yeast (13:18-21). The point is the same, and it is told twice so that no one can miss it: God searches, and God rejoices. Some Christians have been surprised to find God pictured as a woman. The early church was not. Gregory the Great, a bishop of Rome around AD 600, preached that the woman in this story stands for God, and the lamp for God's wisdom shining in a human life.

The coin cannot do anything to be found. It cannot even know it is lost. The whole story is about the one who searches.
passages.ot:
The Scriptures more than once picture God's love as a mother's. “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb? Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” (Isaiah 49:15). “As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13).

And the prophets speak of God's own joy over his people: “He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing” (Zephaniah 3:17).
passages.hard: Is God a woman, then? The Bible calls God Father, and Jesus taught his followers to pray ‘Father’. But it also uses a mother's love, and here a woman's search, as pictures of who God is. Christians confess that God is neither male nor female, as human beings are, and that all these pictures are true pictures of one God. The church's prayers keep the names the Bible gives; the stories show how wide God's love is.
passages.asks: The coin was lost inside the house. Some people are lost not out in the hills, but at home, in church, in plain sight. Ask who near you might be lost in that way. And ask whether you believe that God would light a lamp and sweep the whole house for you.

passages.t: A son who left, and came to his senses
passages.happening:
Then Jesus says, “There was a man who had two sons” (verse 11). The younger son says, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So the father divides his property between them.

A few days later the younger son gathers everything he has and goes off to a distant country. There “he squandered his wealth in wild living” (verse 13). When it is all gone, a severe famine strikes, and he begins to be in need. He hires himself out to a man of that country, who sends him into his fields to feed pigs. He longs to fill his stomach with the pods the pigs are eating, “but no one would give him a thing” (verse 16).

At last “he came to his senses” (verse 17). Even his father's hired workers have more than enough food, and here he is starving. He decides to go back and say, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants’ (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story. It is often called the parable of the prodigal son. ‘Prodigal’ means wasteful. But the story begins with ‘a man who had two sons’, and it is as much about the father, and the older son, as about the younger.

Under the Law, the firstborn son received a double share of what his father left (Deuteronomy 21:17). With two sons, the younger would get a third. Normally a son received it when his father died. A father could hand out his property while he was still alive, but it was not wise. A Jewish wisdom book called Sirach, written about two centuries before Jesus, warns a father not to give his property away while he lives, in case he needs to ask for it back. So the younger son's request was unusual, and it broke the honour a son owed his father. The story does not say what the father felt. It says only that he gave it. And he divided the property between both sons (verse 12), so that later he can tell the older one, ‘all that is mine is yours’ (verse 31).

The son turns his share into money and leaves. A ‘distant country’ was far from home and family, and from the land of Israel. The pigs show where he is: among people who were not Jews. Under the Law pigs were unclean, not to be eaten (Leviticus 11:7). For a Jewish young man to tend another man's pigs, and to envy what they ate, was about as low as he could fall.

The pods were most likely carob pods, the long bean-like fruit of the carob tree. They were cheap food for animals, especially pigs, and very poor people ate them when there was nothing else. He wants even that, and no one gives it to him.

‘He came to his senses’, literally ‘he came to himself’. Hunger makes him think. His speech is honest about what he did: he has sinned against heaven, which means against God, and against his father. Readers have wondered whether he is truly sorry or only hungry. The story does not settle it. What it shows is that he turns toward home. What happens next does not depend on how good his speech is.
passages.ot:
The prophets called Israel home with words like these: “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled by your iniquity. Bring your confessions and return to the LORD” (Hosea 14:1-2). And God promised, “I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them” (Hosea 14:4).

God asks through Ezekiel, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23).
passages.hard: Does the younger son earn his way back by deciding to come home? The story says he ‘came to his senses’ and turned toward home, and that matters: Jesus has just spoken of ‘one sinner who repents’. To repent is to turn around. But he planned to come back as a hired worker, and the father never lets him finish that speech (verse 21). He is welcomed as a son before he has made anything right. The turning matters. The welcome is a gift.
passages.asks: The son only saw clearly when he had nothing left. Ask whether there is some ‘distant country’ you have gone to, a place, a habit, a way of living, that has left you empty. And notice what he remembered when he was starving: not his own goodness, but his father's house. Ask what you remember about God when everything else runs out.

passages.happening:
So he gets up and goes to his father. “But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him” (verse 20).

The son begins his speech: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son’ (verse 21). But the father does not let him reach the part about being a hired servant. He calls to his servants: “Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!” (verses 22-24). And they begin to celebrate.
passages.hearers:
The father sees him ‘while he was still in the distance’. He must have been watching the road.

Then he runs. In Jesus' world, a man of standing did not run. The site's portrait of honour and shame in the Bible's world sets out the evidence carefully. Kenneth Bailey, who taught for many years in the Middle East, argued from the village life he knew there that a dignified older man in long robes did not run in public, so the father takes the shame of the road on himself. That is a modern parallel, not ancient evidence. But the ancient ideal of dignity points the same way: the Greek philosopher Aristotle said that a great-souled man walks slowly and speaks in a deep, even voice, because hurry belongs to someone who takes too many things seriously. This father takes one thing very seriously. He runs to his son in front of everyone, and he throws his arms around him and kisses him before the boy can say a word.

The son's speech is cut short. He never gets to say ‘Make me like one of your hired servants’. The father does not argue with him. He simply calls for the signs of a son.

The best robe, a ring and sandals: these do not dress a hired hand. They dress a son. When Pharaoh raised Joseph to honour, he put his ring on Joseph's finger and dressed him in fine linen (Genesis 41:42). The father gives his son back his standing in the household, in front of the servants, before anyone else can rule on it.

A fattened calf was kept for a great day. It was far more meat than one family could eat, so the feast would be for many. The father's words are the centre of the whole chapter: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!” The sheep, the coin, and now the son. Each story ends in a party.

The painter Rembrandt painted this moment: the old father bending over his kneeling son, his hands on the son's back.
passages.ot:
When Jacob came home after years away, afraid of the brother he had wronged, “Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept” (Genesis 33:4). The father does the same three things.

And God speaks of his people as a parent: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him” (Psalm 103:13). “Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me, a delightful child?” God asks. “Therefore My heart yearns for him; I have great compassion for him” (Jeremiah 31:20).
passages.hard:
The father forgives without any sacrifice or payment. Does that mean the cross was not needed? This is a real question, and it has been asked from more than one side. Some readers have said that this story is the whole gospel: God is a Father who forgives the one who comes home, and nothing more is needed. Jewish readers have rightly pointed out that the prophets taught the same welcome long before (Hosea 14).

Christians have answered in several ways. Many note that a parable makes one point, not every point. This one answers the grumbling of verse 2 by showing God's joy over one who comes home. It does not explain how God's forgiveness is made possible, just as it says nothing about the Holy Spirit or the resurrection. Luke himself says more elsewhere: Jesus speaks of ‘the new covenant in My blood’ (22:20), and after rising he says that the Christ had to suffer, and that forgiveness is preached in his name (24:46-47). Others find the cost inside the story itself: a father who bears loss, public shame and grief to bring both sons home, a picture of costly love that points toward the cross. And many add that the man telling the story was himself the welcome it describes, eating with sinners on his way to die in Jerusalem.

So the story shows plainly that God runs to meet the sinner who turns home, and that his welcome is free. It is not the whole of what the New Testament says about the cross. Christians explain the cross in more than one way (see the note on Mark 10:35-45), and these notes do not choose among them. What all agree on is what the father shows: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

A word to anyone whose own father was not like this one. If your own father was absent, or hurt you, this story is not asking you to pretend otherwise. It tells you that you have a Father in heaven who is not like that.
passages.asks: Ask what you expect God to say if you come back to him: a lecture, a test, a place among the servants? Jesus says the Father is already watching the road, and that he runs. Ask what keeps you in the distant country, if it is not his welcome.

passages.t: The older brother outside the door
passages.happening:
Meanwhile the older son is out in the field. Coming near the house, he hears music and dancing. A servant tells him, ‘Your brother has returned, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has him back safe and sound’ (verse 27).

The older son is angry and refuses to go in. “So his father came out and pleaded with him” (verse 28). The son answers, “Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!” (verses 29-30).

‘Son, you are always with me,’ the father says, ‘and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found’ (verses 31-32).

The story ends there.
passages.hearers:
Here is the reason for the whole chapter. The Pharisees and scribes were grumbling that Jesus welcomed sinners (verse 2). The older brother grumbles that his father welcomed his brother.

He has a point, and Jesus lets him make it. He did stay. He did work. He never shamed his father in a far country. A young goat for a few friends against a fattened calf for a crowd: it feels unfair. Many readers feel for him, and they are meant to.

But listen to how he speaks. He calls his years at home ‘serving’, like a hired worker, the very thing his brother had planned to become. He will not say ‘my brother’; he says ‘this son of yours’. And he adds the prostitutes, which the story itself never said (verse 13 says only ‘wild living’). He is as far from his father's heart as his brother was, without ever leaving home.

And look at the father. He leaves his own feast, as he left his house for the younger son, and goes out to the older one. He ‘pleaded with him’. He calls him ‘Son’; the Greek word is a tender one, ‘child’. He does not take back what is his: ‘all that is mine is yours’. And he gently changes ‘this son of yours’ into ‘this brother of yours’.

Then the story stops. We are not told whether the older brother went in. Jesus leaves the door open, and the Pharisees standing at it.
passages.ot: The prophet Jonah was angry when God forgave the people of Nineveh. “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger,” he complained (Jonah 4:2). His book, like this story, ends with God pleading with an angry servant and a question left unanswered.
passages.hard:
Is the older brother a picture of the Jewish people? For centuries many Christian preachers said so: the older son was Israel, jealous of God's grace to the Gentiles, and the younger was the church. As early as the 200s the North African Christian writer Tertullian noted that many read it that way, and he argued that the details do not fit. That reading has fed contempt for Jewish people, and it is wrong. Everyone in the story is Jewish, the younger son as much as the older, and so was everyone listening, the tax collectors and sinners included. The father loves both sons and goes out to both.

The older brother is not a picture of the Jewish people. He is anyone who has stayed close to God's house and grown hard toward those who come home late, and the church should see itself in him first. He is the faithful church member who resents the newcomer, the long-serving Christian who keeps a quiet tally of what God owes them, the believer who would rather be right than glad. Jesus told this story to religious people, and it still speaks first to them.

Is God unfair to the son who stayed? The father says no: ‘all that is mine is yours’. Nothing was taken from the older son by his brother's welcome. Grace given to someone else is not a loss to you.

A word to parents. Mary and Joseph lost their son for three days and did not understand his answer. If you have a child who has wandered or whom you cannot understand, you are not the first. This story does not promise that every child will come home, or say when. It shows what kind of Father God is: one who watches the road, runs to the one who comes back, and goes out to plead with the one who will not come in. Keep the door open as far as you safely can, and keep praying. God has not stopped loving your child, and he has not stopped loving you.
passages.asks: Every reader is somewhere in this story. Ask honestly which son you are most like today: the one who left, or the one who stayed and grew hard. And if you are the older brother, hear the father's voice: ‘Son, you are always with me.’ The music is still playing. Will you go in?
